hints: Look closely at the smallest side of each block, not just the overall size. Which block is the thinnest?
For the whole block to turn colourless, acid must diffuse all the way to the centre. Think about which shape gives the shortest diffusion distance to the middle.
walkthrough:
**Understand what colour change means**

Think of this as a diffusion experiment. The acid outside must diffuse into the agar to turn the pink indicator colourless.

The block is only fully colourless when acid has reached the very centre.

**Spot the key factor: diffusion distance**

Diffusion is slow over long distances. The time taken depends most on how far the acid has to travel to the centre.

That distance is set by the thinnest dimension, because acid can enter quickly from the two large flat faces.

**Compare the thinnest side of each block**

Block A is only $3 \text{ mm}$ thick, so acid only has to travel about $1.5 \text{ mm}$ from each large face to reach the middle.

Blocks B, C and D are $6 \text{ mm}$ or $12 \text{ mm}$ thick, so the distance to the centre is $3 \text{ mm}$ or $6 \text{ mm}$, much further. Therefore block A is penetrated right through most quickly and becomes colourless first.

options.A: Correct. At only 3 mm thick with very large flat faces, acid has the shortest distance to diffuse to the centre, so the whole block turns colourless most quickly.
options.B: Not fastest. Although this small cube has a high surface area to volume ratio, it is 6 mm thick, so acid must travel further to the centre than in A.
options.C: Slower than A. It is 6 mm thick, so the diffusion distance to the centre is twice that of block A.
options.D: Slowest. This is the largest, thickest block at 12 mm in every direction, so acid has the longest distance to travel to the centre.
